extracted.intended_audience: American colonists (general public and political leaders) in late 18th century
extracted.subtask_description: A persuasive political pamphlet setting out reasons, practical considerations, and prescriptive recommendations for American independence and the formation of Continental government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity over numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not in numbers, but in unity, that our great strength lies; yet our present numbers are sufficient to repel the force of all the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Continent's whole united force is decisive; a single colony cannot support itself but the whole when united can accomplish the matter. Emphasizes political unity as the central measure of readiness for independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present timing — 'the time hath found us'
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquiry into the ripeness for independence ceases because 'the time hath found us' — a general concurrence and union of things proves the fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that current confluence of circumstances (military experience, union, resources) makes now the appropriate time to declare independence; delaying will make accomplishment harder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of land forces and need for naval capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Our land force is already sufficient; with unity we can succeed, but naval affairs must be addressed since Britain would not allow an American man of war while continent remained under her control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes land and naval readiness: land forces are adequate now; naval capacity can be developed domestically (shipbuilding, timber, iron) and is strategically necessary for defense and commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naval self-reliance and shipbuilding suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: No country is so happily situated to raise a fleet as America — tar, timber, iron, and cordage are natural produce; ship-building is America’s natural manufactory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat building a fleet as commerce: build ships to use or sell, replacing paper currency with gold/silver. Emphasizes domestic materials and skill; historical examples given (ships built in New-England forty years ago).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicality of manning ships with landmen
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary that one fourth part should be sailors; a few able sailors can instruct active landmen in common ship work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses privateer example to show small number of sailors can train others, so manpower shortages should not deter naval efforts; current unemployed shipwrights and sailors make this feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: National debt as acceptable if used to establish government
rubrics_metrics.description: Debts we may contract do not deserve our regard if the work (establishing an independent constitution/government) be accomplished; a national debt is a national bond and, when it bears no interest, is not a grievance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues the cost of independence is justified; compares to Britain’s large debt and navy; suggests sale of western/back lands to pay debts and support government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sale of back lands to discharge debt and support government
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of back lands can be applied to sinking the debt without burden to any, and the quit-rent reserved will always lessen and in time support the yearly expense of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical fiscal proposal: sell unoccupied lands now rather than allow the king to dispose of them; Congress to act as continental trustees for these sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continental Charter as solemn bond protecting rights
rubrics_metrics.description: A charter is to be understood as a bond of solemn obligation which the whole enters into, to support the right of every separate part, whether of religion, personal freedom, or property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offers the Continental Charter as the foundation document protecting religious freedom, personal liberty, and property; presented as a principled compact among the parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large and equal representation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is necessity of a large and equal representation; a small or unequal number of electors or representatives is dangerous and can concentrate power unjustly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives example of Pennsylvania where a small number of members could have governed the province; warns against trusting concentration of power and stresses representative breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful mode for choosing Congress; separation of powers of representation and election
rubrics_metrics.description: The mode for choosing members of Congress deserves consideration; questions whether representation and election is not too great a power for one and the same body of men to possess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies institutional design should avoid concentrating selection and control in the same body; calls for planning for posterity and not making virtue hereditary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious liberty protected by government
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the indispensable duty of all government to protect all conscientious professors of religion; diversity of religious opinions is beneficial and should be protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Urges throwing aside narrowness and suspicion; views different denominations as children of the same family and government’s role limited to protection of conscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Youth and small population as advantages for forming government
rubrics_metrics.description: The infant state of the Colonies is an argument in favour of independence: fewer numbers mean more land unoccupied and more unity; youth is the seed-time of good habits for nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that earlier union will produce more lasting concord formed in adversity and infancy; warns that later population and commerce would create diversification of interests and weaken union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreliability of British protection — do not expect future safeguarding
rubrics_metrics.description: Can we expect Britain to protect us after reconciliation? A navy thousands of miles off is of little use in sudden emergencies; conquest may be effected under pretence of friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues practical impossibility and danger of relying on British protection; recommends self-defense instead of reliance on former oppressor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diplomatic benefits of independence
rubrics_metrics.description: While we call ourselves the Subject of Great-Britain, no power can offer mediation; independence will allow foreign courts to receive and hear us and make mediation possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommends publishing a manifesto to foreign courts explaining grievances and asserting peaceful trade intentions to gain support and recognition abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconciliation is complicated, untrustworthy, and insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconciliation is a matter exceedingly perplexed and complicated, involving a treacherous capricious court; independence is a single simple line contained within ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that even if Britain granted concessions, future parliaments could repeal them; reconciliation cannot guarantee redress of burned towns, losses, and debts; independence is more secure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for clear seat of government to prevent usurpation
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping vacant the seat of government opens a door to eternal tyranny — if the seat is not legally and authoritatively occupied, some fortunate ruffian may fill it and threaten freedom and property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates forming government 'at the right end' (charter first, then executors) to avoid being forced to accept laws from conquerors; warns of dangers of leaving power unorganized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal security: define status of combatants and traitors
rubrics_metrics.description: A line of distinction should be drawn between English soldiers taken in battle (prisoners) and inhabitants of America taken in arms (traitors); traitors forfeit life, prisoners do not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues for legal clarity regarding insurgents and combatants to maintain order and discipline; implies necessity of laws to distinguish and punish appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of arms justified only for defense of persons/property
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking up arms is justified when it is defense against violence to persons and property (invasion by fire and sword); not justified to enforce repeal of a pecuniary law alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral criterion: the value of human life limits use of force; use of arms becomes conscientious when necessary for defense against physical violence, and the era of independence is dated from first musket fired in defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine commerce and defense (premiums to merchant-built armed ships)
rubrics_metrics.description: If premiums were given to merchants to build and employ ships mounted with guns, fifty or sixty such ships with a few guardships would keep up a sufficient navy without burdening the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy proposal to link commercial incentives with naval defense in peacetime so as to maintain a ready force economically and avoid the peacetime decay of a standing navy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dependence on foreign navies; exploit geographic advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Though Britain’s list of ships is formidable, not a tenth are fit for service at once and their distant stations give America the advantage on her own coast where proximity yields two-to-one advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic point: a smaller, locally-focused naval force can outmatch a globally-deployed navy because of shorter lines of communication and concentrated defense of home waters.
